name: backend-for-frontend
context: Multi-client distributed systems where different frontend applications (mobile, web, desktop, TV) have divergent data requirements, performance constraints, and authentication flows. The BFF pattern introduces a dedicated server-side service between frontend clients and backend microservices, tailored specifically to each client type's needs. This pattern is particularly relevant in microservices architectures where backend services are organized by domain rather than by client experience.
benefits: Client-optimized responses with data shaped specifically for each frontend
Bandwidth efficiency for mobile clients through minimal payload sizes
Frontend team autonomy over their API layer without backend dependencies
Technology flexibility allowing each BFF to use different languages or frameworks
Isolated changes where modifications to one client don't impact others
Fault isolation ensuring one client's BFF failure doesn't affect other clients
Support for complex client-specific features like real-time updates and offline support
tradeoffs: Code duplication across BFFs for similar aggregation logic
Additional infrastructure overhead for deploying and monitoring multiple services
Requires frontend teams to have full-stack capabilities
Consistency challenges when backend APIs change
Added latency from the intermediary layer
Increased operational complexity with multiple deployment pipelines
use_cases: Mobile applications requiring bandwidth-optimized payloads and aggressive caching
Web SPAs needing rich data aggregation and real-time updates via SSE/WebSockets
Admin portals requiring different auth flows and data access patterns
Desktop applications with distinct data requirements from mobile/web
Partner APIs needing different rate limiting and response formats
IoT/device clients with severely constrained bandwidth and battery considerations
avoid_when: Only one client type exists and no plans for additional clients
Simple authentication sufficient for all clients
All client types have identical data requirements and update frequencies
Operational maturity is low (no CI/CD, monitoring, or distributed tracing)
Client requirements are stable and unlikely to diverge
component_types: Client-Specific BFF Service: Dedicated backend per client type (mobile, web, desktop) that owns the API contract and evolves independently
Data Aggregator: Combines and transforms data from multiple backend services into a single client-optimized response
Protocol Adapter: Translates between client protocols (REST, GraphQL, WebSocket) and backend protocols
Authentication Facade: Handles client-specific auth flows (OAuth/PKCE for mobile, sessions for web, API keys for internal)
Caching Layer: Client-optimized caching strategies with appropriate TTLs for domain and user data
Error Normalizer: Transforms backend errors into client-friendly, consistent error responses (RFC 9457 problem details)
Data Transformer: Converts data formats, date types, field names, and payload shapes for specific client needs
technology_stack: Node.js, Express, NestJS, FastAPI, Azure Functions, AWS Lambda
Kong, AWS API Gateway, Azure APIM, NGINX
REST, GraphQL Federation, gRPC, Server-Sent Events
Distributed tracing (Jaeger, Zipkin), structured logging, correlation IDs
design_principles: Client-Specific Optimization: Each BFF should be tailored to its specific client's needs, optimizing data shape, payload size, and delivery mechanism
Thin Orchestration Layer: BFFs should only aggregate, transform, and normalize—no business logic that belongs in domain services
Stateless Design: BFFs should be stateless to enable horizontal scaling behind load balancers without complex session management
Clear Ownership Boundaries: Frontend teams should own their respective BFFs end-to-end: code, deployment, monitoring, and on-call
Explicit API Versioning: BFF APIs must be versioned to support multiple client versions simultaneously, especially for mobile apps with long update tails
Cross-Cutting Concerns Separated: Monitoring, logging, rate limiting, and authorization should be abstracted or handled via API Management
